analysis.one_liner: Strips state and local governments of the power to block new natural gas hookups.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in the final days of the 117th Congress with no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states, cities, and state utility regulators from banning new or restored connections to the natural gas system. Several localities have passed such bans as part of building-electrification policies aimed at cutting emissions and shifting new buildings to electric heat. The bill would override those policies in favor of keeping gas service available everywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas utilities and makers of gas furnaces, stoves, and water heaters, which would be guaranteed a market for new hookups even in places trying to electrify buildings. New construction customers — especially landlords and developers who prefer gas equipment — would also keep that option open.

how_it_helps.text: It bars states, local governments, and state utility regulators from prohibiting a natural gas consumer from connecting or reconnecting to a gas utility [S2][S3].
For existing gas customers, it guarantees the option of reconnecting to gas service if a locality's electrification rules would otherwise cut them off [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would lose a tool they have used to cut building emissions and steer new construction toward electric heat. Households and renters in jurisdictions with electrification goals would continue to add gas-burning infrastructure with its emissions and, over time, gas system costs spread across remaining customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local electrification efforts and climate goals

drawbacks.text: The strongest case for it: bans on new gas hookups take away a real choice from homeowners, landlords, and developers who may find electric heating equipment costlier to install or a poor fit for their buildings.

It is a federal preemption of local land-use and utility decisions: a single federal rule would override what cities and states have decided about building electrification, and it would keep gas-burning infrastructure in buildings despite local climate and public-health policies [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does preserve a genuine consumer option — gas service — where some governments have tried to phase it out. But its main effect is to lock the gas system's role into every new building nationwide, overriding local electrification policies. The cost falls on governments' ability to set their own building standards and, ultimately, on emissions and the customers who share the gas system's fixed costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last week of the session, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs introduced the bill on December 16, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept their authority to restrict new gas hookups — though only because the bill was too late and too lightly supported to move, not because it was voted down.

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting state and local bans on natural gas connections.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill sat there with no markup or hearing
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill guarantees gas utilities a right to serve customers in every state and locality, blocking the local hook-up bans that shrink their customer base. It keeps gas infrastructure in new buildings even where cheaper electrification policies exist, which is why the industry's interest in this bill runs against local climate policy.

industries.industry: Gas heating and cooking appliance makers
industries.note: By preventing bans on new gas connections, the bill preserves demand for gas furnaces, stoves, and water heaters that local electrification rules would otherwise phase out. The cost lands on emissions and on households that share the fixed costs of the gas system.
